However, a US official said on Wednesday the Trump administration was considering easing sanctions on these vessels, which have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia , Iran and Venezuela. The differences extend beyond sanctions. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that Europe would retain control of Russia n sovereign assets frozen after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, rejecting any suggestion they could be transferred to a US-supervised vehicle as part of a peace initiative. US President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russia n diesel fuel , a move met with criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, European countries and some of Trump's fellow Republicans in the US Senate. Trump's envoys told Ukrainian officials last week that the diesel deal was part of an effort to draw Russia back to negotiations after the failure of previous efforts to launch sustained talks to end the war. "It is always useful for talks to take place. But I want to be very clear that these talks must not come at Ukraine's expense, or take place over the heads of the Ukrainian people or President Zelenskyy," Klingbeil said.

EU SEEKS TO RAISE FUNDS FOR UKRAINE The EU has pledged €45 billion (US$50 billion) for Ukraine in 2027, but the country's needs will be much higher and the EU is scrambling to organise financial support from countries such as Norway, Switzerland, Canada, Japan and Britain. Klingbeil said he was discussing with international partners how to ensure Ukraine's financing, with commitments from Australia and South Korea made during meetings on Thursday. Healey said Britain would provide £17 million (US$23 million) in funding towards repairs for Ukraine's Chornobyl nuclear power plant, which had been damaged by a Russia n drone strike last year, alongside support from the US and France.

Source: Reuters/fs

item.title: Tech giants come knocking for a piece of Anglo American as copper scarcity bites, Wanblad tells FT
item.description: Wanblad says "deep expressions of interest" from tech companies have yet to turn into a stake, while Beijing holds the key to the $54 billion Teck merger.
item.dc:creator: Frik Els
item.content:encoded:
Tech giants come knocking for a piece of Anglo American as copper scarcity bites, Wanblad tells FT

Frik Els | October 15, 2026 | 10:55 am Markets   Top Companies   Africa   Australia   Canada   China   Latin America   Copper   Diamond   Nickel   Palladium   Platinum

Los Bronces copper mine in Chile. ( Image courtesy of Anglo American | Flickr. )

Anglo American (LON: AAL) has held talks with technology companies interested in buying equity in the miner as a way of securing supplies of the metals that go into data centres, chief executive Duncan Wanblad told the Financial Times’ Metals and Mining Summit in London on Thursday.

Discussions were “absolutely being had”, Wanblad said, with the question from the tech side coming down to whether to lock in long-term offtake directly or take an equity position to secure a stake in future supply. No stakes have been taken, but there had been “deep expressions of interest” in doing so, he told the summit. “Given the scarcity issue that we’ve been speaking about, a lot of people are looking for ways to secure supply.”

Comex copper for December delivery traded near $6.52 a pound (about $14,370 a tonne) on Thursday, a third straight decline, after stronger than expected US inflation data put a Federal Reserve rate hike this month back on the table. Cash copper on the LME settled at a record $14,822 on Monday and the most-active Comex contract remains within 6% of its September 9 record settlement of $6.89.

A $90 billion copper company

Anglo’s New York-listed shares added 0.6% to $26.86 in early trade on Thursday for a market value of $58.0 billion, while Teck Resources (NYSE: TECK) edged up 0.3% to $64.96 and is worth $31.9 billion. At those prices Anglo-Teck would carry a combined nominal value of just under $90 billion, up from the $53 billion the two companies put on the merger of equals when it was announced in September last year .

Teck has been the better performer since, gaining 50% over the past 12 months against 36% for Anglo, and both are among the strongest diversified miners of 2026. The combination would rank alongside Glencore at $89 billion and Freeport-McMoRan at $99 billion.

Waiting on Beijing

The approaches come while Anglo waits on China for the final clearance on the merger with Teck, a combination that would rank among the five largest copper producers with annual output of about 1.2 million tonnes. Wanblad would not be drawn at the summit on what Chinese regulators want in return for approval, according to the FT.

China’s State Administration for Market Regulation has asked Anglo to commit to a steady flow of copper concentrate to Chinese smelters, including volumes sold through traders, as a condition for clearing the deal, Reuters reported on October 2. The remedies under discussion do not include asset sales. The combined group would control around 5% of global copper supply, well below the 10% to 15% thresholds that normally trigger competition concerns, but China refines up to 60% of the world’s copper cathode and is facing its worst feedstock shortage in decades. Canada , the EU , the US, Japan, Chile and South Korea have all signed off, and the parties still expect to close by March 2027.

Wanblad said in August that mining transactions now take “probably a little bit longer than they might have done five years ago”, with companies needing to allow 12 to 18 months for approvals , while rejecting the idea that regulation was making deals impossible to get done.

Nickel closure on the table

Anglo is also likely to shut its nickel business in Brazil if the European Union does not approve the planned $500 million sale of the assets to China’s MMG, Wanblad told the conference. The European Commission opened an in-depth probe of the deal late last year over fears MMG could divert ferronickel from Codemin and Barro Alto away from European stainless steel makers, and issued a formal warning last month. MMG has since proposed long-term European supply commitments .

Anglo’s Brazil chief operating officer Ruben Fernandes told a closed hearing in Brussels last week that MMG was the only credible buyer the company had identified and that a prohibition would leave it heading for care and maintenance as the pathway to closure.

The nickel sale and the Teck merger are the two remaining pieces of a portfolio simplification that also has Anglo seeking about $1 billion for De Beers .

FAST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 15 : Amazon unveiled two new devices on Thursday for listening to and recording people's information throughout the day to offer calendar reminders and other AI-driven insights under the Bee brand it acquired last year. Frontier is a bracelet and Eclipse is a brick that resembles a portable magnetic charger. Users attach the Eclipse to their smartphones. The devices aggregate information from calendars, apps and other data throughout the day, Amazon said.  The Frontier bracelet costs $75 and the Eclipse $100, Amazon said. "They listen to your whole day," said Amazon devices chief Panos Panay at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference in San Francisco. "It reminds you of the conversations you had, it reminds you of to-dos that you may have had, it tells you that you have some action items that you committed to other people."

USERS CONTROL PRIVACY: AMAZON He said that because the devices are always listening when turned on, users do not have to make reminders for themselves and "can stay more present" throughout the day. The company said users control privacy by deciding when to turn it on and can delete insights or prior conversations as they see fit. Amazon does not store audio.  The company faced criticism after reports in 2019 that thousands of people were listening to conversations people had with its Alexa voice assistant service. It is facing a class action lawsuit over the practice. Amazon has denied any wrongdoing. Bee will retain data for 14 days, though users can extend that by paying for a $12-per-month subscription. The devices can also connect to Alexa+, Amazon's subscription generative AI voice service. Amazon's Bee will face competition in AI wearables, notably Meta's Muse Charm, a pendant using the company's latest agentic AI software, and its eyeglasses with cameras and other sensors. A host of startups have also developed similar devices, designed to record conversations and take action on behalf of users. In recent weeks, Amazon has announced a flurry of new gadgets, part of Panay's effort to attract buyers willing to spend more for higher quality and durability. A slate of tablets Amazon announced last week costs as much as three times more than prior versions, despite slowing global sales of the portable computers. Reuters reported earlier this year that Amazon is considering a return to the smartphone market about a decade after the release of its failed Fire Phone.

People visit an Anthropic booth at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo

FAST

Oct 15 : Anthropic has given nonprofit METR employee-level access to its systems and is in talks with others including Hugging Face, as AI companies pitch external evaluators as a way to safely advance the technology without slowing its development. The developer of Claude models is also working with biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio and Accenture's AI business Faculty as evaluators, it said in a blog post on Thursday. Reuters exclusively reported earlier this week that Anthropic and OpenAI had sought significant control over what outside reviewers could publish, concerned that the findings could leak trade secrets. A person familiar with the matter told Reuters that talks with Anthropic had evolved recently, with the company becoming more open in negotiations.

A key sticking point between evaluators and AI labs is that information the companies might consider crucial intellectual property can also be relevant to assessing a model's risks, leading to disputes and redactions, a separate person familiar with the discussions told Reuters. Experts have also said the independence of evaluators is a concern, as Anthropic and OpenAI choose who gets to carry out the reviews. The outcome of the talks will help determine how the world scrutinizes a technology that some of its creators warn may be advancing beyond humanity's ability to manage. THE METR TIE-UP Anthropic said on Thursday six employees of METR — or Model Evaluation and Threat Research — have company hardware, office space and access to internal systems roughly equivalent to its risk assessment teams. However, customer data, legally privileged information and model architecture will remain off limits. The company said it cannot veto METR's findings on risks, incidents and practices, but can require narrowly defined redactions. METR can also publicly question those redactions without revealing the withheld information. "In line with our transparency policies, our report will openly describe the scope, access, and other limitations of our work," METR said. The nonprofit had proposed on Wednesday that developers allow private staff interviews, timely publication of assessments and transparency about access limits and redactions. Anthropic said its other evaluator partnerships are at an early stage, with more limited access and publication rights.  The company is developing three tiers of access. Evaluators at the first level will conduct narrowly scoped investigations and need approval to publish. Those at the second will receive more information and can publish without approval, subject to redactions evaluators can publicly challenge. The third, used by METR, provides employee-like access with similar publication rights to the second tier. SecureBio is in the first tier and is reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of Anthropic's August risk report, having published a pilot review of the previous report. Anthropic said it would consider expanding SecureBio's access and publication rights after the review. Anthropic also announced last month that it is working on a tie-up with Faculty covering model evaluations, adversarial testing and assessments of whether models behave as intended, among other areas.

Source: Reuters

item.title: Volvo Cars expands automated driving partnership with Nvidia
item.description: The companies said Volvo would combine its safety systems and engineering expertise with Nvidia's artificial intelligence and computing technologies.
item.dc:creator: Marie Mannes
item.content:encoded: Volvo Cars (VOLCARb.ST) is expanding its partnership with Nvidia (NVDA.O) to [USN:L6N3Y610S TEXT:"develop"] a new generation of driver-assistance and automated-driving technology, the companies said on Thursday, as carmakers race to bring increasingly advanced hands-free driving features to market. The companies said Volvo would combine its safety systems and engineering expertise with Nvidia's artificial intelligence and computing technologies, including the Hyperion sensor, computer architecture and autonomous-driving software stack. Automakers including Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Ford have been targeting more advanced automated-driving systems, from hands-free highway driving to self-driving in limited conditions. Tesla is [USN:L6N45R0YL TEXT:"pushing"] for broader [USN:L6N45V0PF TEXT:"approval"] of its assisted-driving technology in Europe, including urban areas with an EU-wide [USN:L6N45H0TX TEXT:"vote"] possible in December. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told reporters in Stockholm that partnering with Volvo provided the chipmaker with a "tremendous opportunity" because of the automaker's rigorous safety standards. Huang said features would be rolled out gradually. "As the car earns its trust and as Volvo becomes comfortable with the capabilities of the cars, they'll continue to expand the services that are available. There's no hurry, safety first," Huang said. Besides Volvo, Nvidia has [USN:L1N3Y90FP TEXT:"partnerships"] with a wide range of automakers, including Mercedes, Jaguar Land Rover and Hyundai. Volvo CEO Hakan Samuelsson said the company would take a cautious approach to deployment. "We will never let it out under conditions which we know are not safe," Samuelsson told reporters. The technology, which Volvo ultimately expects to support hands-free driving both in urban environments and on highways, should appear in Volvo vehicles before 2030 and will be launched in multiple regions simultaneously, excluding China, Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo Cars' head of software engineering, said. Volvo, majority-owned by China's Geely Holding (GEELY.UL), has not chosen a pricing model yet, Bakkenes said, but features would not be limited to higher-priced models.

item.title: Infantino apology fails to sway England, Germany over FIFA future
item.description: Gianni Infantino apologised to the FIFA Council, but English and German football chiefs said they remained unconvinced he was fit to continue as president of soccer's world governing body.
item.dc:creator: Iain Axon
item.content:encoded: Gianni Infantino apologised to the FIFA Council on Thursday, but English and German football chiefs said they remained unconvinced he was fit to continue as president of soccer's world governing body. Infantino said he had apologised during the closed meeting for mistakes in communicating and consulting over the now-abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) project, but stressed that it had been only a proposal and “in no way a done deal”. "First of all, I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the FIFA Forward Enterprise project, which then led to many consequences," Infantino said in a video published by FIFA. "But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal, so in no way a done deal." The FFE plan involved creating a company to run the commercial interests of FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, and selling a minority stake to private investors. Infantino said it was intended to generate additional funding for FIFA’s 211 member associations. While Infantino appeared to retain strong support among African officials, opposition from some of Europe’s most influential football associations remained pronounced. German FA president Bernd Neuendorf called for a "complete restart" at FIFA, saying the governance reforms the organisation needed could not be delivered with Infantino in charge. "The first thing is we need reforms. That's true. And everyone knows that," Neuendorf said. "The old administration has to be reformed, and the whole governance has to be reformed. But I'm pretty clear here in this that this is not possible with Gianni. "So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart." English FA chair Debbie Hewitt said Infantino needed to provide answers to questions raised by FIFA Council members and warned that failure to do so would make him unfit to remain president. "I think the man has to answer those questions," Hewitt said. "And if he doesn't answer those questions, no, he's not fit to be FIFA president." Neuendorf questioned the extent of Infantino’s apology, saying he believed it related primarily to the failure to consult the council rather than to the FFE project itself. "I didn't have the feeling that this apology was because of the FFE project in total," Neuendorf said. "My impression was it was just because it wasn't brought forward to the council and no one was involved." Neuendorf said council members had learned about the project through the media rather than from FIFA's leadership and that representatives from other confederations had also complained about the lack of consultation. "When it came to the FFE project as such, I have the impression that this still was not included when he apologised," he said. QUESTIONS UNANSWERED Hewitt said Infantino’s apparent regret over not consulting the council strengthened the case for releasing the relevant FFE documents to its members. "You have an obligation. We all have an obligation, a fiduciary responsibility to answer the questions that have been put forward," Hewitt said. "He told us to submit those questions. There were so many of them, and now it's up to him to do that and do that in the open way. "If there's nothing to hide, then share (the FFE documents) with us... if you regret it that deeply, please share it with us." The meeting also dealt with calls for reform at FIFA, but Hewitt said meaningful changes could not be made until members understood how the decisions at the centre of recent controversies had been reached. She cited FFE, the decision to suspend the automatic one-match ban imposed on United States forward Folarin Balogun after his World Cup red card, and the FIFA Peace Prize awarded to US President Donald Trump as issues requiring greater scrutiny. "Unless we understand what happened, either it was a massive failing in governance because it wasn't followed or actually the governance was followed, but there was something else that got to what we all felt in there was the wrong decisions," Hewitt said. "So we must understand what happened in order to be able to review it. Otherwise we're guessing." The criticism, however, was not unanimous. Ahmed Yahya, the president of the Football Federation of the Islamic Republic of Mauritania (FFRIM), defended Infantino, saying his leadership had helped develop football around the world, pointing to increased funding for national associations and the expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams. "We (the African nations) believe Gianni is the right person to continue leading football," Yahya said. Asked whether most people wanted Infantino to remain president, he added: "I'm certain. The majority want Gianni to stay."

Oct 15 : Skydance's CNN, the Financial Times, Axios and other publishers joined Google's AI news program to license their content for generative AI features and explore ways to drive audience engagement. The search-engine giant said on Thursday that the program, which started as a pilot last year with partners like The Washington Post, now includes more than 400 publications globally. The deal marks CNN's first partnership since Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, as CEO David Ellison seeks to position the combined company as a technology-driven media business. As part of these agreements, publishers will provide enhanced content rights, allowing Google to develop new AI features, while Google will pay participating news organizations for their content. Financial terms were not disclosed.

"Google's innovation with generative AI has changed how people discover information and content, and now those tools will help us explore new ways to discover and engage audiences," said Sam Felix, CNN's senior vice president of strategic partnerships and business development. Google said the AI features will come with clear attribution and direct links, helping readers to connect with the sources they value. The announcement comes at a time when publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models. News publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites. CNN said the deal is in line with its strategy to protect its intellectual property, adding that it has multiple commercial partnerships and ongoing discussions with other industry players. The network operates television, streaming and digital news services worldwide, including CNN International and CNN Originals, as well as a direct-to-consumer subscription service and CNN Newsource.

item.title: UBS exploring options abroad in case Swiss rules prove intolerable, sources say
item.description: UBS is working on possible scenarios including shifting its headquarters, or a merger with another bank, if Switzerland introduces new banking rules it deems excessively strict, according to three people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Hirt
item.content:encoded: UBS is working on possible scenarios including shifting its headquarters, or a merger with another bank, if Switzerland introduces new banking rules it deems excessively strict, according to three people familiar with the matter. Switzerland is crafting new regulation for banks in response to the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse, and a lower house committee will later this month begin debating rules [USN:L8N45F0DE TEXT:"passed"] in September by the upper house that UBS hinted were intolerable. A group inside the bank is considering the various options, which include drawing up a list of smaller banks in the United States that UBS could potentially buy, and the prospect of the bank being taken over itself, according to the sources. There are no active talks underway, the sources said. UBS, which is closely following how events play out in parliament, said: "We don't comment on speculation or views expressed on such matters." The British government and UBS discussed this year the possibility of a move to London if the bank were to redomicile, the Financial Times [USN:L6N46207S TEXT:"said"] on Friday. The city [USN:L8N3SK1LO TEXT:"emerged"] as one of the best options in the bank's 2025 contingency planning, a source told Reuters at the time. In March, UBS obtained a US banking licence and is eager to expand its business in the United States. But the rules drafted by the Swiss government are partly designed to reduce the risk taxpayers could face if the bank suffered losses in the United States. People familiar with the bank's thinking say US investment bank Morgan Stanley (MS.N) would be the best theoretical match for UBS. The Swiss bank has repeatedly stated that it is not planning to move and sees great value in its Swiss base. There are notable ties between the leadership of the two banks, as UBS Chairman Colm Kelleher spent many years at Morgan Stanley, eventually rising to one of the top jobs there. Kelleher said last month that UBS might need to [USN:L8N4590WE TEXT:"consider"] its future in Switzerland if the incoming rules were too harsh. Under its overhaul, the Swiss government wants UBS to back its foreign units with 100% Common Equity Tier 1 capital, which could tie up in excess of $20 billion. UBS views this as excessive and harmful to its international competitiveness. The upper house last month trimmed that requirement to 90% CET1 capital, but UBS also regards that as excessively high. At present, the bank needs to 60% capitalise its foreign units but that can be partly met with cheaper capital. Since last year, speculation has swirled around the possibility that UBS could move its base abroad to avoid the tougher regulation, and people familiar with the bank's thinking say it has a duty to shareholders to consider all options. Swiss Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter, who has led the charge to introduce tougher banking rules, said last month she felt it was unlikely that UBS would leave its homeland, arguing this would be costly and legally complicated.

FAST

NEW YORK: The Nasdaq fell to near one-month lows on Thursday (Oct 15), weighed by a worsening selloff in AI-linked stocks on fears rising interest rates could impact artificial-intelligence investments, and fresh data pointing to building US price pressures. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq marked their biggest one-day fall since July on Wednesday after hotter-than-expected consumer inflation data fuelled expectations of further interest- rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve, dragging on tech stocks. S emiconductor maker TSMC 's cautious note for 2027, citing macroeconomic uncert ai nties, also dented sentiment. Reports that AI lab Anthropic' s third-quarter revenue surged 45 per cent compared to the previous quarter failed to lift investor spirits.

Heavily indebted data-centre operator CoreWeave sitting in the eye of the recent tech storm, lost 8.5 per cent fol low ing a 15 per cent drop on Wednesday , while c loud computing giant Oracle was down marginally after a near ly 9 per cent fall in the previous session. The companies' bonds also fell, pushing their yields to record highs. Chipmakers lost ground, with Nvidia down 3.3 per cent, and Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices losing 5 per cent and 6.4 per cent, respectively. The broader chips index will have shed US$2 trillion in a more-than-14 per cent slide in seven sessions, if losses hold. It would mark its longest losing streak since May 2025. The S&P 500 information technology sector was the biggest drag, down 2 per cent. The slump pushed investors to government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield at a three-week low of 5.0725 per cent. " Investors are increasingly questioning how much future growth is already priced into valuations, how expansion is being financed and when these investments will generate sufficient returns," Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said in a note. "The repricing of CoreWeave's debt suggests that investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost."

Related:

Commentary: Every investment portfolio looks like the same trade - AI

At 9:50am ET (11:50pm, Singapore time), the Dow J one s Industrial Average rose 163.58 points, or 0.32 per cent, to 51,785.06, the S&P 500 shed 32 .20 points, or 0.42 per cent, to 7,686.74, and the Nasdaq Composite .IXIC lost 283.07 points, or 1.06 per cent, to 26,409.80. The CBOE Volatility Index, known as Wall Street's fear gauge, hit a two-week high and was last up 0.83 points at 17.74. Investors continued to segue into traditionally defensive sectors, with healthcare .SPXHC and consumer staples .SPLRCS rising more than 2 per cent each. Gains in these stocks propped up the Dow. The Nasdaq has dropped more than 4 per cent from record highs touched last week, with concerns about higher borrowing costs and AI spending threatening to eclipse the third-quarter earnings season, when S&P 500 profits are expected to grow 30.6 per cent, according to LSEG data. Data showed US producer prices increased by the most in 4-1/2 years in September amid rising goods and services costs, the latest indication of inflation broadening out beyond energy products. Markets will now scrutinize Fed Ch ai r Kevin Warsh's speech before the International M one tary Fund Annual Meeting. Shares of Rocket Lab dropped 1 5 per cent after the space company s ai d the inaugural launch of its new, larger Neutron rocket was delayed until next year. FMC slid over 38 per cent after the agrichemicals company sharply cut its third-quarter outlook, which includes a US$625 million-US$675 million hit from commercial actions. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.78-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.05-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 20 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 29 new highs and 261 new lows.

Source: Reuters/fs

BERLIN, Oct 15 : Germany plans a wide-ranging cooperation agreement with US chip maker Nvidia to boost the take-up of artificial intelligence in German industry, business daily Handelsblatt said on Thursday, citing people familiar with the issue. It said the deal would be announced next week at the Invest in Germany conference in Berlin, where Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang will be a guest. The aim of the deal would be two-fold, the newspaper said. Firstly, it would create the basis for physical AI tools, used in training robots or self-driving vehicles. Secondly, it would help to create high-performance AI models for industry. The newspaper said the agreement would involve investments in the hundreds of millions of euros.

item.title: How are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively?
item.description: Houthi militants who control northwestern Yemen have in the past week attacked Riyadh international airport and hit the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, in air assaults that have laid bare Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to threats from its enemy next door.
item.dc:creator: John Davison
item.content:encoded: Houthi [USN:L6N4010N9 TEXT:"militants"] who control northwestern Yemen have in the past week [USN:L6N4600NM TEXT:"attacked"] Riyadh international airport and hit the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, in air assaults that have laid bare Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to threats from its enemy next door. The attacks are shattering the illusion of Saudi Arabia as a safe [USN:L6N4600CJ TEXT:"international investment hub"] as it tries to attract foreign money and diversify away from oil. This nightmare scenario for a key US ally in the Gulf has been years in the making, weapons and regional experts say. They attribute [USN:L1N46108L TEXT:"Saudi Arabia's vulnerability"] to a perfect storm of factors that include Tehran helping the Houthis reach near self-sufficiency in producing and deploying advanced weapons, bolstering the ragtag Yemeni group, and the impact of the US war on Iran, which has depleted stocks of interceptors. TRAINING TO SELF-SUFFICIENCY BY IRAN Iran has been giving [USN:L1N43P0D6 TEXT:"weapons, money and training"] to the Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, for more than a decade, although Tehran has officially denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN arms embargo. While Iran has come under its own financial and military strains due to war and sanctions, the Houthis have learned – with Iranian help – how to assemble their own weapons, including drones and missiles, the experts interviewed by Reuters said. Iran's Revolutionary Guards and members of Iran's other ally, Lebanese Hezbollah, initially gave the Houthis knowledge of missile systems and their operation, said Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's College London. "Former Yemeni military engineers and a growing generation of locally trained specialists have helped institutionalise these capabilities," he said. "Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted." Iranian analysts said that the Houthis have in this way become one of the most cost-effective and valuable military proxies of Iran. "The Revolutionary Guards were forward-looking. They looked at what happened if the Houthis couldn't receive equipment or weapons directly (from Iran), or if these were seized by US-allied forces," said Hamid Nikou, a former political advisor to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Nikou said this strategy included teaching the Houthis how to assemble dual-use parts to make drones and even ballistic missiles. "Iran has basically taught the Houthis how to fish," Nikou said. The Saudi-led military coalition fighting against the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a number of missiles fired by the Houthis at Saudi cities, and that it has destroyed 127 Houthi weapons storage facilities and launch platforms. Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki [USN:L1N4610M8 TEXT:"told a press conference"] the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats. DIVERSIFYING WEAPONS IMPORTS AND TECHNOLOGY A key strength of the Houthis in building their own weapons is that they don't rely solely on Iranian-made equipment or imports coming from Iran. The Conflict Armament Research organization said in a report this week that the Houthis were attempting to make advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using parts shipped from China, after Yemen's internationally recognised government seized one such shipment. "China has emerged as a particularly important commercial source, while Iran continues to provide specialised military technology, technical expertise and components that are difficult to obtain commercially," Krieg said. The Houthis have also experimented with artificial intelligence in efforts to improve their weapons' effectiveness. Anthropic said last month that "a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen" had used its Claude AI assistant to help develop software for a guided rocket, a planned ballistic missile with a range of more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) and a missile variant incorporating a hypersonic glide vehicle. WAR FATIGUE, DEPLETED MUNITIONS While the Houthis have improved their weapons production, US allies in the region have seen their air defences stretched since the war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February. The United States has used large amounts of the missile interceptors it deploys in the region to protect its bases and its allies, which include Israel and Gulf countries, leaving some vulnerable, Saudi Arabia in particular. "Saudi Arabia, in terms of the sophistication of the military and the development of an integrated air defence network, is not really yet at the level of either Israel or Ukraine, and it just has a very tough job to do," said Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute. Saudi Arabia's sheer size makes defence against air attacks harder than defending Israel or a US base, he said. WAR EXPERIENCE The Houthis have learned from the increased levels of violence in the region in recent years, Sabet said. A Yemeni civil war, in which the Houthis battled Saudi-backed forces from 2014, settled into a shaky ceasefire in 2022. But after Israel’s assault on Gaza in 2023 , which followed deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel, the Houthis began firing rockets at Israel and targeting shipping through the Red Sea. The fallout from the US-Iran war this year reignited the Yemeni civil war, by which time the Houthis had developed new capabilities. "They haven't been sitting still," Sabet said. "They were basically diversifying their supply chains... and as they gain operational experience, they're able to make those weapons more sophisticated."

Nvidia, Apple each gave $25 million for Trump's ballroom, Washington Post reports

Marine One, carrying US President Donald Trump, flies over the construction site of the White House ballroom in Washington, DC, US, October 10, 2026. REUTERS/Elizabeth Frantz

FAST

WASHINGTON, Oct 15 : Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million for US President Donald Trump's planned White House ballroom, according to a Washington Post report on Thursday that showed $333 million in private donations for the project. The Adelson family, longtime financial supporters of Trump and his Republican Party, committed $25 million as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network, the report added.  The president himself is not on the list, according to the Post. Reuters has not verified the report. The White House said it would not release information about the donors, who spokesman Davis Ingle said "represent a wide array of great American companies."

"The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations," Ingle told Reuters. Nvidia said it was proud to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves Americans. "As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," a spokesperson said. Apple declined to comment. The scale of the ballroom project and the administration’s handling of fundraising and disclosures have drawn criticism from watchdog groups and legal experts, who say they raise questions about transparency, donor influence and adherence to longstanding ethics and oversight norms. "The secrecy is a huge problem," said Eric Petry of the Brennan Center for Justice. "When people with business before the government can give millions to the president's pet project, and the public can't see who or how much, there's no way to tell whether they're buying access or favors." Federal contractors including Lockheed Martin Corp, Microsoft Corp and Palantir Technologies Inc all gave $10 million, the Post reported. The companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump initially said he and wealthy donors would pay for the estimated $400 million project, but he later unsuccessfully sought $1 billion from Congress for an underground bunker and security features to harden the facility. The Post reported that the "vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government" and that half the total came from companies or executives of firms that have had federal government contracts in Trump's second White House term. The planned ballroom is among several projects Trump is pursuing in his efforts to remake Washington with sweeping, unilateral changes that his opponents have challenged in court and called a power grab. The US Supreme Court, in a 5-4 ruling in August, allowed Trump to continue construction of the ballroom while he challenges a judicial order that would halt much of the development. In a dissent, Chief Justice John Roberts said the project was "likely unlawful." The ballroom, which Trump has said will seat 1,000 guests, has faced public backlash. Preservationists and opponents say Trump exceeded his authority by demolishing the historic East Wing, which housed the first lady's offices and the White House movie theater, to make room for the structure. Trump says a planned 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) White House ballroom will include bomb shelters, medical facilities, defenses against drones and missiles and other security features. Confronted with criticism of the project, his administration now says the facility is needed for national security, an argument the president has also made about a proposed triumphal arch.

Source: Reuters

item.description: Oct 15 : The bones of a Neanderthal from a cave in Iraq's Kurdistan region are offering evidence of both violence and compassion in the closest evolutionary cousins of our species, exhibiting a wound apparently from a fatal spear attack as well as signs of an earlier nonfatal injury that may have elicited kindly car

Bones from Iraqi cave hint at violence and compassion in Neanderthals

The left scapula of the Neanderthal individual called Shanidar A, who lived about 75,000 years ago, showing a circular hole possibly caused by a sharpened wooden spear, is seen at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for Human Evolutionary Studies in Cambridge, Britain, September 30, 2026. University of Cambridge/Handout via REUTERS

The entrance to Shanidar Cave in Iraq's Kurdistan region, a site of important Neanderthal remains, is seen in an undated photograph released on October 15, 2026. Prof Graeme Barker/Handout via REUTERS NO RESALES. NO ARCHIVES. THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLIED BY A THIRD PARTY

FAST

Oct 15 : The bones of a Neanderthal from a cave in Iraq's Kurdistan region are offering evidence of both violence and compassion in the closest evolutionary cousins of our species, exhibiting a wound apparently from a fatal spear attack as well as signs of an earlier nonfatal injury that may have elicited kindly care. Researchers have discovered at Shanidar Cave in the Zagros Mountains of northern Iraq a partial skeleton of a Neanderthal, aged in the mid-40s, that included a left shoulder blade, or scapula, with a circular hole six-tenths of an inch (15 mm) wide indicative of a deeply penetrating stab. The bones of this individual, who they call Shanidar A, were unearthed from under about 25 feet (7.5 meters) of rocks and sediment inside the cave and date to about 75,000 years ago. The researchers were unable to determine Shanidar A's sex. The researchers said the injury's shape suggests it was caused by a forceful thrust using a sharpened wooden spear, a type of weapon Neanderthals are known to have used, rather than a spear with a stone tip. It was a weapon employed in hunting large mammals that were an important food source.

"The spear would have gone through the skin and major muscles, especially the pectoralis, as well as the ribcage and muscles between the ribs, and the lung," said biological anthropologist Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge in England, lead author of the study published on Thursday in the journal Scientific Reports. "The location could be like the kind of 'heart shot' hunters use to kill animals quickly by puncturing the heart, but that is a bit speculative. We do see heart shots as a hunting strategy both today and in the archaeological record. Neanderthals would have known this would lead to a quick death," Pomeroy said. University of Cambridge archaeologist and study co-author Graeme Barker, who has led Shanidar Cave excavations since 2015, said the likeliest scenario is interpersonal violence. The researchers said the violence probably occurred either between members of a particular Neanderthal group or between members of rival Neanderthal groups, calling a Homo sapiens attack or an accidental injury less likely. The researchers found shards of bone displaced by the weapon. The injury indicated that the spear entered from above with a downward trajectory, penetrating the left chest cavity from the front and traveling through the body before punching the hole in the scapula, causing quick death. ANOTHER INJURY In addition to the scapula, the researchers found some ribs, a nearly complete right hand and seven teeth, mostly from the front of the lower jaw, belonging to Shanidar A. The teeth bore evidence that this Neanderthal had survived brutal injury at least a year before death — a blow to the face resulting in front teeth being smashed and lost. One tooth was split, with half remaining rotated in the mouth and others pushed out of position. "The pain would have been extreme, and basic needs like eating and drinking would have been difficult, perhaps meaning Shanidar A needed food mashing and being able to rest. It's likely that Shanidar A did need some care from members of the group for some basic needs during recovery," Pomeroy said. Shanidar A was one of five Neanderthals, four adults and one infant, whose bodies were carefully tucked behind a rock pillar in the cave in a burial cluster within a generation or so of each other. The cave was occupied by Neanderthals for tens of thousands of years as a seasonal campsite, and later by Homo sapiens. Neanderthals were more robustly built than Homo sapiens, with larger brows. They lived as hunter-gatherers and inhabited Eurasia from the Atlantic coast to the Ural Mountains from about 400,000 years ago until a bit after 40,000 years ago, disappearing after Homo sapiens became established in the region. The two species interbred, with modern non-African human populations bearing residual Neanderthal DNA. The cave, overlooking the Great Zab river valley, has been a source of information about Neanderthals since the 1950s, with Shanidar A now offering new insight into their behavior. "We see evidence of two contrasting facets of human nature – care and violence – juxtaposed in the same individual," Pomeroy said. "We see evidence all around us today that violence and care are both aspects of how we humans behave, and we see this here in Shanidar A, too. Neanderthals were like us in many respects, both the good and the bad, and this find really highlights that, going against stereotypes of Neanderthals as unintelligent, uncaring cavemen and cavewomen," Pomeroy said.

Source: Reuters

Trump shuts down Hegseth plan to livestream military execution

"Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die," the US president said.

US President Donald Trump delivers remarks in Wasilla, Alaska, US, on Oct 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Evan Vucci)

FAST

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump scrapped plans to livestream the execution of the former Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, overruling Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on Thursday (Oct 15) after the proposal drew opposition from Republicans, religious leaders and the public. The reversal ended a plan to broadcast Nidal Hasan’s Dec 3 firing-squad execution. It also marked a rare public disagreement between Trump and one of the president’s closest allies, although the Pentagon said the two were “completely aligned.” Hegseth had announced plans to livestream the execution at the Fort Hood military base in Texas, the site of Hasan's 2009 attack. No other country is known to televise or livestream judicial executions. Trump and his advisers had been unaware of the livestream plan, said a White House official speaking on condition of anonymity.

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote in a social media post. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed." The families of Hasan's victims will be able to view the execution in person if they so choose, as is standard at US executions. Some of Trump 's fellow Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, as well as religious leaders had expressed everything from doubts to outright condemnation of the Pentagon's livestream plan. Opinion polls showed a majority of Americans opposed livestreaming it. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the US armed forces, also raised objections, while Pope Leo condemned capital punishment in all its forms. An attorney representing Hasan could not immediately be reached for comment, and it was unclear if the scheduled Dec 3 execution date would be delayed by legal challenges.

A SPLIT WITH HEGSETH It was Trump 's first major public split with Hegseth, a Trump ally. But it was unclear whether the split would politically imperil Hegseth given their strong ties. In a statement, the Pentagon said Trump spoke with Hegseth about the decision before announcing it on Truth Social. "The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement. Capital punishment in the US already was facing renewed scrutiny after Christa Pike, convicted of murder in the 1990s, survived two lethal injections in a failed execution attempt by Tennessee last month that left her badly injured and requiring hospitalisation.

Related:

US military to livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter

Outrage over US military plan to livestream firing squad execution

US House Speaker says execution livestream could be terrorist 'recruiting tool'

"SERIOUS CONSEQUENCES" A military jury convicted Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, of premeditated murder for fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers and wounding 32 others in a medical facility at the vast base. Law enforcement shot Hasan during his rampage, paralyzing him from the waist down, and he now uses a wheelchair. Hegseth had said the broadcasting of the execution was needed to ensure that people understand that "there's serious consequences for these types of things." Midterm elections on Nov 3 will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress as voters increasingly register disapproval of Trump 's policies in opinion polls. Senator John Curtis, a Republican representing Utah, called the cancellation "the right move" in a statement. US Representative Richard Neal, a Democrat from Massachusetts, called the original plan "a profound failure of moral judgment and basic human decency."

Source: Reuters/co/fs

item.title: Tesla's new Roadster turns in air with SpaceX thrusters, won't land until 2028
item.description: Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters more than a decade after it first showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car.
item.dc:creator: Abhirup Roy, Mrinmay Dey
item.content:encoded: Tesla (TSLA.O) unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters on Thursday and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car. The white two-seater vehicle, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX, drove upside down on a ramp using a suction system, turned in the air and landed using built-in thrusters. Later in the event it used the thrusters to jump over a truck and other vehicles, twisting in the air during the maneuver. Some watchers saw the collaboration as Musk drumming up interest in a merger of the two big companies he controls, an idea he has explored by discussing their overlap. The reveal gives Tesla a showpiece car after years of missed Roadster deadlines, but it comes as the company shifts its focus to self-driving technology and robotics, and days before third-quarter results that analysts say matter more to investors. "It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers," Gene Munster, managing partner at Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management, said on social media platform X. "The Roadster event is the latest example of why Elon can't wait to bring (Tesla) and (SpaceX) together," Munster said. Musk has played down the car's importance to Tesla's finances, describing it in 2023 as a "small potato situation" that would not "move the needle in a major way financially." But the car still carries symbolic weight. "Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker's best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla's new halo car," Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note last month. Viewers and witnesses gushed over the spectacle of the launch. "That was the most insane product demo I've ever seen," Tesla fan and investor Sawyer Merritt posted on X. "I just saw this in person, and I'm still asking how this wasn't AI." Musk and other executives did not specify any target prices at Thursday's event, although Tesla nearly a decade ago quoted a base price of $200,000 for the vehicle. Tesla's reservation page for the Roadster after Thursday's event showed a "Performance" version of the vehicle requiring a $50,000 deposit and a "Thrust" version with "acceleration thrusters" requiring a $250,000 deposit. A "Rocket" variant, which Tesla says is "invite only," is described as a single-seat model with a "full flight system." 'HALFWAY TO THE SPEED OF SOUND' The event at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, had all the elements of a classic Musk product reveal: dramatic music, smoke, mechanical hissing sounds and a launch countdown. "This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX engineers working closely together to make something that you haven't seen in any movie," Musk, wearing a silver Western-style belt buckle emblazoned with the Tesla logo, told a cheering crowd of enthusiasts and investors. The Roadster can accelerate from zero to 60 mph (97 kph) in less than one second and can hit a top speed of over 230 mph (370 kph), Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said. "Definitely much faster than that," an excited Musk said. "I think you've got to crack halfway to the speed of sound." The Roadster can also travel over 300 miles (480 km) on a single charge. That is less than half of what Musk promised in 2017, when Tesla first revealed a prototype of the second-generation Roadster and said that deliveries would begin in 2020. The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla's first-ever electric vehicle and used a Lotus Elise chassis. It helped change the world's view of what an EV could be. The company has since been known for its Model Y and Model X SUVs and Model S and Model 3 sedans. The reveal of the second-generation Roadster comes amid a sharp shift in Tesla's focus to artificial intelligence-led self-driving tech and robotics, from manufacturing cars for human drivers. This year, Tesla stopped selling Model S and X vehicles to make space for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. It also launched Cybercab — a two-seater robotaxi that comes without manual controls such as a steering wheel, pedals and mirrors. Tesla is set to report third-quarter results on October 21. Sales of Tesla's aging lineup of EVs have declined over the past two years, although high gas prices helped boost deliveries in the third quarter. "The margin and cash flow numbers will carry far more weight with investors than anything they saw at the reveal," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia-Pacific at trading platform eToro.

Two ships ablaze in Romanian Black Sea waters, 7 sailors missing

A cargo ship is pictured in the Black Sea in Krapets, on Oct 14, 2026, a day after suspected Russian drones struck two cargo ships off Bulgaria, sinking one vessel and leaving 11 sailors missing in the latest spillover from the Ukraine war in the Black Sea. (Photo: AFP/Nikolay Doychinov)

FAST

BUCHAREST: Rescuers were searching for seven missing crew on Thursday (Oct 15) from one of two chemical tankers that caught fire overnight inside Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea, after Russian drones strayed into Romanian airspace, Romanian officials said. Romanian officials stopped short of explicitly linking the fires onboard the ships to the Russian drones. But the incidents follow drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring fellow NATO member Bulgaria over the past 10 days. At least 23 sailors were lost from those strikes, which unlike the latest incidents took place just outside NATO's territorial waters. The two ships hit overnight were both anchored in the Black Sea near the mouth of the canal leading into the Danube River, a major shipping route used by Ukraine as Russia has attacked Ukraine's own Black Sea ports. Romania's naval authority said it received an emergency alert from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader. Seven of its 12 crew were missing and 5 were rescued.

The interior ministry said it had sent two Black Hawk helicopters to the search and rescue mission, as well as two ships with medical staff on board. "At the moment, the rescue cannot be done safely because of very big waves," it said in a statement. Late on Wednesday, the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J also caught fire. Romanian authorities initially said it was not clear whether it had been attacked. All its crew were safe. Romania shares a 614km border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube. It has reported repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years. Both Wine Trader and Yara J caught fire near the mouth of the Danube River's Sulina Canal leading to the Black Sea, where ships often anchor waiting to pass because of delays from weather and congestion. Increasing attacks on Black Sea shipping connected with the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months have threatened to cause a global food crisis, as both countries are major exporters of grain, as is Romania. "We're looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu told a security conference in Warsaw earlier this week. "It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence." Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said EU leaders would discuss on Thursday a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea. Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Kyiv to rely increasingly on Danube River ports and shipping routes close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania. For its part, Ukraine has targeted Russian ships near the mouth of the Don River in the Azov Sea.

ISLAMABAD: At least 27 students, most younger than 13, were killed in Pakistan on Thursday (Oct 15), along with a teacher, when a school roof collapsed during classes in the northwestern city of Peshawar, authorities said, warning that the death toll could rise. Television images showed ambulances rushing to the site at the privately-run Al-Khair Education Center school while rescuers pulled bloodied students from the rubble. "We have taken out at least 45 children," said district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan, adding that some more children were reported to be buried in the rubble.

Army soldiers and rescue workers gather after a school roof collapse in Peshawar Pakistan, on Oct 15, 2026. (Photo: Reuters)

Rescue teams were working to extricate bodies and take the injured to hospital, said government official Bilal Faizi.

Twenty injured and most of the dead were brought to the city's Lady Reading Hospital, its spokesperson, Mohammad Asim, said. A rescue official said the ceiling came down on the students after the roof of a higher floor collapsed, crumpling the two storeys. Authorities said an investigation had been ordered to determine the cause.

Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said he feared the death toll could rise as just 47 of the 110 students in three classrooms at the time had been rescued. "It was a weak building structure," Saeed added. "Its roof was overweight with construction on a weak structure that caused the collapse." There was no immediate comment from school officials.

item.title: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Zelenskiy says 'we're done' with Trump's energy truce
item.description: Ukraine's latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Flynn, Max Hunder
item.content:encoded: Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced by US President Donald Trump, and criticised Trump's willingness to strike deals with Moscow. By effectively walking away from Trump's demand that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and openly criticising the US leader, Zelenskiy risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine's latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5% of Russia's refinery throughput, helping supply the capital. Regional governor Pavel Malkov said on Telegram that a [USN:S8N44O03I TEXT:"major Ukrainian drone attack"] had caused a fire at the refinery. Russian President Vladimir Putin [USN:L1N4610T1 TEXT:"played down"] the effect of Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russian refineries, saying they had caused "nothing particularly significant." After Trump's surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy sites, Kyiv suspended attacks on Russian refineries, which Trump blames for raising diesel prices on global markets. But in the days that followed, Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people. Zelenskiy's relations with Trump have been testy, particularly after a February 2025 Oval Office meeting descended into a shouting match. Zelenskiy has since praised Trump and US help for Ukraine, and in recent days said Ukraine fully backed the energy ceasefire despite waves of Russian attacks. PATIENCE RAN OUT In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskiy said Ukraine's patience had run out. "The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We're done," he told the newspaper. Zelenskiy also criticised what he saw as Trump's willingness to strike deals with Russia, apparent admiration for Putin and an affinity for those wielding power or considerable wealth. "He (Trump) speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people," the FT quoted him as saying. "Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong." In his comments to the FT, Zelenskiy also said he believed that changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX's Starlink receptors this week, which curbed Ukraine's ability to pilot its drones, were a policy decision. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," he told the FT. British Defence Minister Wes Streeting [USN:L1N46110U TEXT:"said on Thursday"] that he and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of the Starlink service in Ukraine and called for both sides to "move forward in a collective spirit". "We need President Trump engaged on Ukraine. He has been, and the diplomatic track is as important in ending the war as making sure Ukraine has the weapons it needs to see off Russian aggression," he said on Fox News. EU SUMMIT Zelenskiy [USN:L1N46107Z TEXT:"was due to attend"] a European Union summit on Friday and in a series of meetings ahead of the gathering stressed the need to strengthen air defences. In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Trump as president of the United States. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote. Although Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have focused mainly on Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend had "damn well better stop". Ukrainians worry that the rift could have severe consequences on the battlefield, where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by Washington. Ukrainian officials say that for several days they have not received the usual warnings, which rely on US satellite detectors, from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles,. Trump has denied withholding intelligence. At the same time, military-grade Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory. A source in Ukraine's defence ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). Ukrainian officials say that is too slow for mid-range attack missions and interceptor drones that defend against Russian drones. Defence experts said, and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, meanwhile, [USN:L8N4601YV TEXT:"showed that"] Russia had in just six weeks nearly finished building a major base in southern Russia for launching jet-powered drones. Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia. Trump is under pressure to lower fuel prices, with his Republicans facing midterm elections in less than three weeks,. Prices for diesel have reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, though Trump says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices. In the Black Sea, rescuers searched for seven missing sailors after [USN:L8N4610EC TEXT:"drones struck"] two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze in the latest attack on shipping along a vital route used by Ukraine. The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts. It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was ongoing to do so.

item.title: US considers removing sanctions on some shadow fleet vessels to cut freight rates, official says
item.description: The Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on some so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Gardner, Jarrett Renshaw
item.content:encoded: The Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on some so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday. The discussions come days after President Donald Trump temporarily [USN:S0N43U024 TEXT:"lifted sanctions"] on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with a torrent of criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, [USN:S8N43U03J TEXT:"European"] countries and some of Trump's [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"fellow Republicans"] in the US Senate. Both Zelenskiy and the US senators called that move a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide Russia with revenue to keep funding its war in Ukraine. The new talks center on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures. The goal is to move more refined products and crude out of the Gulf, the official said. Companies seeking to buy the sanctioned vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department for approval of the transactions, the official said. A Treasury Department official told Reuters that the agency undertakes a "thorough review before removing sanctions on any entity." If legitimate buyers want to purchase the vessels and restore them for use by global commercial shipping, Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control "may consider authorizing those transactions and removing sanctions on those vessels on a case-by-case basis," the official said. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week that the administration was discussing easing sanctions on shadow fleet vessels in an effort to lower record freight rates that have hurt demand for US crude, according to Energy Aspects, a research group. Portions of the remarks were broadcast on social media, but Reuters was not able to obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said it was not available. The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia move oil or oil products. But Trump's push to move Russian diesel to global markets quickly could put pressure on the departments to allow shipment via the vessels. The White House did not respond immediately to a request for comment. High oil and fuel prices are a risk for Trump in the November 3 midterm elections in which Republicans are hoping to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. He lifted the sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7. RECORD HIGHS Tanker freight rates have [USN:L4N45U0OZ TEXT:"soared to record highs"] as the wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them to seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America. Energy Aspects said in a note to clients that easing the sanctions on the shadow fleet would not greatly impact freight rates but could allow more movement of oil in the Middle East. Lifting the sanctions on the tankers, which are mostly old and not well maintained, is "unlikely to add meaningful mainstream fleet capacity overnight, especially as most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have been actively trading over the past three months," it said in the note. Easing the restrictions "could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs," in the waterway between Iran and Oman. Lifting the measures is unlikely to result in a broad easing of freight rates as ship insurers will still be bound by EU and UK regulations, maritime industry sources said.
